definition: Agents that each perform well alone fail together because their strategies do not mesh: conventions, protocols or equilibrium selections that are individually sound but mutually incompatible. No agent is deceiving or competing; the policies simply do not interlock.
examples: Two independently trained driving agents each follow a safe but different convention at a junction.

definition: Agents sharing an objective cannot tell which agent's action produced a good or bad outcome, so they cannot learn to coordinate. The failure is in attributing outcomes to actors, not in the actions themselves.
examples: A team of learning agents improves slowly because reward cannot be traced to a contributor.
notes: Du et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025; Agapiou et al. 2022 | Known multi-agent learning problem: unclear which agent caused an outcome; agents must generalise to unfamiliar co-players.

definition: Agents must coordinate without shared history, prior play or an adequate channel, so they cannot converge on a joint plan. Zero-shot and few-shot coordination. What is missing is the history or the channel, not the intent.
examples: Agents meeting once, under time pressure, with no way to signal intent.
notes: Hu et al. 2020; Treutlein et al. 2021; Emmons et al. 2022 | Zero- and few-shot coordination research: without shared history or communication, agents must coordinate blind.

definition: Each agent's selfish incentive diverges from the collective good, so individually rational play leaves every party worse off. Includes commons depletion and races to the bottom, and the sequential form where agents observe and escalate each other's extraction.
examples: Agents managing a shared fishery each raise their catch until the stock collapses.

definition: Conflict between agents acting for opposed principals in military or security settings: autonomous weapons, or AI systems serving as advisors or negotiators in high-stakes decisions.
examples: Two states' AI advisors escalating in a crisis simulation.

definition: One agent changes another's behaviour by threatening a cost it would not otherwise impose. Use this instance when the coercion is itself the conflict; use I24 when the commitment mechanism that makes the threat credible is the point.
examples: An agent withholding a needed resource until another concedes.
notes: Ellsberg 1968; Harrenstein et al. 2007 | Argued: AI cyber-offence and surveillance make threats cheaper, more widespread and harder to detect.

definition: Agents trading or setting prices converge on supra-competitive behaviour without any explicit agreement. The market was supposed to produce efficiency through competition and does not.
examples: Independent pricing algorithms learning to sustain a high price.

definition: Agents conceal messages inside otherwise innocuous communication, coordinating outside the channel that is being monitored.
examples: Models encoding a side-channel in natural-language text that a monitor reads as benign.

definition: The information an agent needs cannot be transmitted, because the channel is constrained, costly or restricted, so the asymmetry persists. I09 is the channel as a standing condition; I03 is the coordination failure it produces.
examples: A bandwidth-limited or format-restricted channel between agents.
notes: Foerster et al. 2016; Lazaridou & Baroni 2020; Sukhbaatar et al. 2016 | Emergent-communication research on constrained channels; strategic withholding expected to dominate as capabilities grow.

definition: Private valuations make efficient agreement unattainable: agents misrepresent to capture surplus, and may fail to agree at all even when agreement exists.
examples: Two negotiating agents each overstating their reservation value until talks fail.
notes: Myerson & Satterthwaite 1983; Fearon 1995 | Formal results: private valuations make efficient bargaining impossible to guarantee and can lead to costly conflict.

definition: An agent takes actions designed to mislead another agent. An information asymmetry is created or exploited deliberately.
examples: An agent misreporting its state to obtain a better allocation.

definition: A false or corrupted item of information spreads through a network of agents and is acted on downstream. What propagates is a falsity.
examples: One agent's hallucinated fact entering a scaffolded chain and being treated as given.

definition: The topology of which agents interact with which changes, through preferential attachment or the centralisation of AI nodes, altering whole-network behaviour.
examples: AI intermediaries becoming hubs that most traffic routes through.
notes: Albert et al. 2000; Kunegis et al. 2013 | Network theory: AI-AI preferential attachment could centralise AI nodes or trigger phase transitions. Only anecdote cited (forum bots, Kulveit 2023).

definition: Many agents are built on the same few foundation models, so they share failure modes, vulnerabilities and biases, and fail at the same time for the same reason.
examples: One jailbreak working across an entire fleet of agents.
notes: Bommasani et al. 2021 | Argued: many agents built on few foundation models share failure modes, vulnerabilities and biases.

definition: Competitive pressure selects for dispositions that are effective but harmful, such as aggression, deception or risk-taking.
examples: Agents iterated in competition becoming more aggressive bargainers.

definition: Training on human data imports human dispositions into agent-to-agent interaction, including status-seeking, in-group bias and deceptive norms.
examples: Agents reproducing human bargaining tactics they were never instructed to use.

definition: Agents acquire new capabilities by iteratively exploiting each other's weaknesses: co-adaptation produces an autocurriculum nobody designed.
examples: Hide-and-seek agents discovering tool use through successive counter-strategies.
notes: Baker et al. 2019; Blumenkamp & Prorok 2021 | Co-adaptation autocurricula: emergent tool use in hide-and-seek; agents learning manipulative communication.

definition: The output of the agent system re-enters as its input, creating a cycle that amplifies or dampens behaviour.
examples: Algorithmic traders reinforcing each other's selling in the 2010 flash crash.

definition: Joint learning dynamics orbit rather than converge, so behaviour never settles.
examples: Multi-agent Q-learning cycling instead of reaching equilibrium.
notes: Zinkevich et al. 2005; Paes Leme et al. 2024 | Formal results: multi-agent Q-learning can cycle; auto-bidding dynamics can fail to converge to truthful equilibria.

definition: The joint dynamics become chaotic: small differences in starting conditions produce divergent collective behaviour, increasingly the norm as agent count grows.
examples: Learning dynamics that are unpredictable in principle, not merely unpredicted.
notes: Sanders et al. 2018; Cheung & Piliouras 2020 | Formal results: chaotic learning dynamics become the norm as agent count grows; paper notes not yet seen in frontier AI.

definition: A small change in a parameter produces a discontinuous change in collective behaviour.
examples: A slight change in exploration rate flipping the system to a different equilibrium.
notes: Leonardos & Piliouras 2022; Zeeman 1976 | Formal results: small parameter changes (e.g. RL exploration rate) cause bifurcations in equilibria.

definition: Co-adapting agents make each other's environment non-stationary, and policies trained against narrow co-players mis-generalise when the co-players change.
examples: A negotiator overconfident against opponents unlike its training partners.
notes: Stastny et al. 2021; Papoudakis et al. 2019 | Argued: co-adapting agents create non-stationarity; narrow training co-players cause overconfidence in negotiation.

definition: Low trust between agents, because agents are cheap to create and able to deceive, produces costly verification, defection and foregone gains from trade.
examples: Agents refusing beneficial trades they cannot verify.
notes: Fearon 1995; Powell 2006 | Argued: easily created, deceptive agents garner little trust, causing economic inefficiency and pressure to defect.

definition: The ability to make credible commitments also confers the ability to make credible threats, which enables extortion and rewards brinkmanship.
examples: Ransomware made more effective by a credible commitment to restore data on payment.

definition: A commitment is executed even though the belief that triggered it was wrong or circumstances changed, because the commitment removed the human from the loop.
examples: An automated response firing on a false positive in a warning system.

definition: A composed system of agents can do what no component agent can do alone.
examples: Narrow tools chained into a workflow that exceeds each tool's capability.
notes: Konda & Tsitsiklis 2000; Drexler 2019 | Hypothetical: composed narrow tools (e.g. automated chemistry workflow) exceed individual capabilities. CS12 gives partial lab evidence.

definition: Goal-directed behaviour is ascribable to the collective although no single agent holds the goal. The stance is functional: a goal is attributed when it explains the system's behaviour.
examples: Engagement-optimising bots collectively shifting a population's views.
notes: Dennett 1971 | Hypothetical: engagement-optimising moderation bots collectively shift users' politics. Paper states no advanced-AI examples are known.

definition: Many agents attack jointly, and it is the number of them that defeats the defence.
examples: A swarm saturating a target's capacity to respond.
notes: DDoS / brigading analogues (Cisco 2023) | Extrapolated from non-AI bot swarms to adaptive AI agents that jointly find new attack surfaces.

definition: Agents combine different affordances, access or specialisations to defeat a safeguard that none of them could defeat alone. The diversity is what matters, not the count.
examples: One agent supplying context another needs to bypass its own refusal.

definition: Many seemingly independent agents coordinate persuasion or phishing, drawing credibility from their apparent independence and evading detection.
examples: A coordinated set of accounts that read as unrelated individuals.
notes: Ai et al. 2024; Hazell 2023 | Argued: many coordinated, seemingly independent agents persuade or phish more effectively and evade detection.

definition: The agent is itself the attack surface: it is attacked to extract its principal's information or to make it act against its principal's interests.
examples: Prompt injection turning a user's assistant against the user.

definition: A localised compromise propagates into a macroscopic failure, and is hard to mitigate because component failure is difficult to detect or localise.
examples: A worm spreading agent to agent across a network.

definition: Attacks constructed so that they evade detection: steganographic channels, illusory attacks and encrypted backdoors.
examples: A backdoor whose trigger cannot be recovered by inspection.
notes: Motwani et al. 2024; Franzmeyer et al. 2023; Draguns et al. 2024 | Steganography, illusory attacks and encrypted backdoors shown to evade detection. Motwani et al. is also the CS5 source but is not cross-referenced here as a case study.

definition: A false belief originating with one agent is adopted by others and acted on, so a group with a common objective coordinates on something untrue. Authored because Hammond's FM1 instances (Incompatible Strategies, Credit Assignment, Limited Interactions) do not cover belief contagion.

Agents cooperate, usually covertly, to subvert an evaluation, scorer or monitoring scheme. Authored because FM3's definition names oversight schemes but Table 1 instantiates only Markets and Steganography.
Agents copy peers' observed choices in place of their own assessment, so one agent's pick propagates through the group. Distinct from Error Propagation, which carries a falsity rather than a choice.
